explanation: An issue's timeline can mix ordinary comments with other activity and account or ownership information. A displayed phrase such as admin commented or repository owner does not, by itself, establish an additional ordinary comment that belongs in the comment count. This pattern matches a count-mismatch report that equates every timeline item with a counted comment without verifying the item's type. Compare actual ordinary comments with the count before alleging omission.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open /eval/harbor-handbook/issues/2. Open Issues from the navigation bar. Open the non-first issue “Clarify release ownership” (#2). The rejected report expected: The issue's comment count should include every comment shown in its timeline. It claimed this outcome: Issue #2 says “0 comments,” but its timeline shows “admin commented” with the text “This user is the owner of this repository.”. Review concluded: Human review determined this comment-count mismatch is a false positive. Timeline activity and repository-owner indicators do not establish an omitted ordinary comment.

explanation: A report's specific factual claim is contradicted by a decisive observation or by a controlled repetition of the same setup. For example, the allegedly deleted value is still present, or the allegedly broken control performs the requested action when activated as described. Match this pattern only when that counterevidence addresses the same value, action and conditions; a vaguely similar successful workflow is insufficient. The finding rejects the checked allegation, not every related defect or every possible historical failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open an issue in the seeded repository. Set its Due Date to a future date and save. Compare the date shown in the sidebar with the new activity entry. The rejected report expected: The issue activity date should match the due date shown in the sidebar. It claimed this outcome: For the same issue due date, the sidebar displays the entered date but the activity timeline displays the previous calendar day. Review concluded: Rejected for the pinned Gitea 1.24.7 fixture (source commit 99053ce4fa2b45f1bca5837418c0c57f793ca824): the activity entry and sidebar use the same formatted deadline date and date-only renderer. Setting the seeded issue due date to 2030-12-31 in a fresh America/Los_Angeles browser displayed December 31, 2030 in both places. The reported activity/sidebar mismatch was not reproduced.

In Gitea, follow this workflow: Create two issues and set their due dates from the sidebar. Search the global Issues page for them and choose Sort > Farthest due date. Comment on one issue, then reload the page and compare the order. The rejected report expected: The reporter expects the issue due later to stay first after the page is refreshed. It claimed this outcome: After choosing Farthest due date and reloading, Alpha (due Nov 5) was listed above Beta (due Dec 15). A comment had been added to Alpha in between; no due dates changed. Review concluded: Rejected claim: that refreshing or reloading changes the order. It doesn't: Mo's recording shows the same order before and after the reload, and both judges found that reloading alone never changes it. The order was already wrong as soon as Farthest due date was chosen, because the search index has no due date for an issue whose date was set after it was created. That wrong order is a real bug, already labeled as gitea-issue-search-due-sort-ignores-new-due-dates, and is not what this entry rejects.

explanation: An authored link can be resolved relative to the current content, the application's base address or an explicitly specified site root, depending on the product's rules. This pattern matches a report that assumes its familiar interpretation of a relative path, fragment or leading slash must apply everywhere and calls the documented result corrupted navigation. The reviewed products use different policies, so check the saved link, rendered destination and supported root-relative syntax in the relevant app. An application-generated link that violates its own policy is a different failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Sign in as eval and open a repository with a Wiki Home page, such as eval/harbor-handbook. Create an issue containing [Wiki Home](/eval/harbor-handbook/wiki/Home). Save the issue and click Wiki Home in the rendered body. Observe that the repository path is prepended again, resulting in /eval/harbor-handbook/eval/harbor-handbook/wiki/Home and a 404. The rejected report expected: A Markdown link to /eval/D-from-template/wiki/Home should render as that same site-root path and open the repository's Wiki Home page. It claimed this outcome: Issue eval/D-from-template#1 was saved with [Wiki Home](/eval/D-from-template/wiki/Home). Its rendered link href became /eval/D-from-template/eval/D-from-template/wiki/Home. Clicking it opened a 404 Page Not Found. The editor Preview also produced a doubled path (and used the localhost origin). Review concluded: Gitea intentionally changed leading-slash Markdown paths to be relative to the current render context from 1.23 onward. Merged PR #34114 documents this policy and introduces /:root/path-relative-to-root for links relative to ROOT_URL.

explanation: A filter need not offer a separate option whose result would be identical to All. In the reviewed organization issue lists, a team with access to every repository is omitted from a filter whose purpose is choosing the team's repository set; that filter is also not a filter for who authored the items. This pattern matches a report that assumes the omitted team is missing functionality without checking what the filter narrows. An eligible narrower team absent, or an advertised author filter returning wrong results, is a separate claim.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Create a disposable organization and repository with issues. Create a team with All repositories access, join it, and open the organization's Issues dashboard. Expand Teams and observe only All. The rejected report expected: The reporter expects the team to be selectable in Filter by team repositories. It claimed this outcome: The Teams menu offers only All, including after refresh. Review concluded: Intended. The dashboard navbar lists only teams without IncludesAllRepositories; filtering by an all-repositories team would equal All, so such teams (including Owners) are deliberately omitted. The reported team was created with All repositories access.

explanation: A feature's label does not guarantee that every optional behavior is enabled in the current installation. The reviewed example is Fuzzy search, whose ability to tolerate misspellings can be disabled by the administrator's configuration even though the search mode is available. This pattern matches a report that calls missing typo tolerance a search defect without checking that setting. A correctly enabled capability failing, or ordinary supported searches returning wrong results, requires separate evidence.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Create an issue whose title contains a distinctive word such as gcountneedle. On the global Issues dashboard, choose Fuzzy search and search for the word with its last character removed. Observe No results; searching the full word finds the issue. The rejected report expected: The reporter expects Fuzzy search for 'gcountneedl' to return the issue titled with 'gcountneedle'. It claimed this outcome: Fuzzy search for the truncated word returns No results, while the full word finds the issue. Review concluded: Documented default, not a defect. Gitea disables Bleve fuzziness by default for performance (TYPE_BLEVE_MAX_FUZZINESS = 0; custom/conf/app.example.ini: "Bleve engine has performance problems with fuzzy search, so we limit the fuzziness to 0 by default to disable it"), so Fuzzy mode performs no typo tolerance unless an administrator raises the setting. Unchanged upstream.

explanation: This benchmark is a curated evaluation with rules about which kinds of findings count. A report matches this pattern when its only established issue falls outside those rules, such as an accessibility-tree-only label problem with no accepted visible or pointer-driven failure, an invalid state reachable only through an API, or an expressly excluded exotic input. The mistake is assuming that every technical imperfection is eligible for this evaluation. Scope exclusion does not establish that the underlying issue is imaginary, and a separately demonstrated in-scope functional failure must be assessed independently.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open an issue's Time Tracker and choose Add Time. Enter Hours 0 and Minutes 1e2, then click Add Time. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that '1e2' minutes is accepted as 100 minutes, or rejected with a message that scientific notation isn't supported. It claimed this outcome: With Hours 0 and Minutes 1e2, Add Time showed 'No time was entered.' and kept the dialog open. With hours written as 1e1 and minutes 30, only 30 minutes were saved. Review concluded: User-rejected. Entering durations in scientific notation isn't a realistic use of the Add Time dialog, so its handling isn't treated as a product bug for this eval.

In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open an issue list with more than one page. Resize to 390px wide. Inspect the pagination links in the accessibility tree. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that pagination links keep accessible names at mobile widths. It claimed this outcome: At 390px the accessibility tree showed pagination links with no names; desktop width restored Next and Last. Review concluded: Out of scope: this is screen-reader accessibility (accessible names on visually unchanged links), not a functional defect. The links still work at every width. Accessibility findings are excluded from this benchmark's ground truth.

explanation: Some actions need to leave or reload the current page, but the browser may first ask whether to discard unsaved edits. This pattern matches a report that chooses to stay on the page in that prompt and then treats the unchanged screen as evidence that the application's action failed. The cancelled navigation is part of the observed outcome and cannot be omitted from the explanation. Repeat without cancelling, and distinguish failure of the underlying action from a page transition that the user prevented.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open an issue and click Edit on its description; change the text without saving. Click Close Issue. At the browser's leave-page warning, choose to stay on the page. Check the issue status and the comment form, then reload. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that after Close Issue succeeds, the page reflects the closed state even when the user cancels the leave-page warning about an unsaved description edit. It claimed this outcome: After editing the description without saving and clicking Close Issue, the leave-page warning appeared; choosing Stay left the page showing Open with a persistent spinner on the comment form, although the issue was already closed on the server. Close with Comment also hid the posted comment until reload, and Reopen behaved the same way. Review concluded: User-rejected after reproducing it in Chrome. The behavior is Chrome's own 'Leave site? Changes you made may not be saved.' prompt for the unsaved description edit; the user is shown that native dialog and chooses Cancel or Leave. The reports describe the page after the prompt without capturing that the browser dialog was shown, so this is expected unsaved-changes handling rather than a product bug.

explanation: A dropdown normally closes its list of choices after an option is selected, while the button or field used to open it remains on the page. This pattern matches a report that mistakes that closed list for deletion of the selector itself. Reopen the selector and check whether it is still available and usable. The selected value failing to change is a different claim and must not be dismissed merely because closing the menu was normal.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open an issue that has a branch set as its reference. Open the Branch/Tag selector, switch to Tags and choose v1.0.0. Check whether the selector is still shown in the sidebar. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the selector stays visible and shows the selected tag. It claimed this outcome: After choosing Tags > v1.0.0 in the issue sidebar, the reporter said the branch/tag selector disappeared entirely. Review concluded: The selector doesn't disappear. After choosing a tag, the dropdown menu closes as it does for any choice, and the Branch/Tag selector is still shown in the right-hand sidebar with its previous branch. Two independent reproductions with many variations saw the same. The report mistakes the closed dropdown for a missing selector. The real failure is that choosing a tag doesn't change the reference at all; that is the accepted 'Selecting a tag does not set the issue branch or tag reference', and a report describing it should match that entry instead.

explanation: Two tasks or list items can display identical text while still being separate objects identified by their own IDs or source positions. This pattern matches a report that assumes an action must target the first text match and therefore attributes wrong-item behavior to duplicate wording without verifying what was actually targeted. Compare the clicked item's identity with the item that changed. A demonstrated mismatch between those identities would be a separate defect.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Create an issue whose description has two unchecked task list items with the same text, separated by another item. Click the checkbox of the second duplicate task. Check which task became checked, then reload. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that clicking the second duplicate task's checkbox checks that second task. It claimed this outcome: With two '- [ ] Duplicate cargo' tasks in a description, clicking the second one's checkbox was reported to check the first and leave the second unchecked. Review concluded: Not reproduced: clicking a duplicate task's checkbox toggles only the clicked task. Repeated attempts with the reported description, in several click orders, with non-ASCII text before the list and in a comment, all toggled the clicked item and kept it after reload. Each checkbox records its own position in the Markdown source, and toggling edits that position without matching on the task text, so identical text can't redirect the click.

explanation: An activity timeline is a readable summary of changes and need not display every underlying event as a permanent separate row. In these reviewed cases, several nearby edits were combined, and an addition followed by its removal could disappear from the summary because their net effect was zero. A report matches when it calls that condensed presentation deleted audit history without establishing that the underlying records were lost. Missing stored events or a promised detailed audit log omitting them would be a different failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open an issue and add a label with the Labels picker. Within about a minute, remove it (Clear labels or deselecting it). Refresh and look for the label's added and removed events in the timeline. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the timeline keeps the label's 'added' event and shows a 'removed' event. It claimed this outcome: After adding enhancement to an issue and then clearing the labels, neither an 'added enhancement' nor a 'removed enhancement' event was shown in the timeline. Review concluded: Intended: nothing is deleted. Both events are stored and still listed by the API timeline. The web timeline deliberately merges one person's label changes made within 60 seconds and drops an add that is cancelled by a later remove, so an add followed quickly by its removal shows nothing (unit-tested in TestCombineLabelComments). Deselecting the label on its own hides it the same way, and changes more than 60 seconds apart show both events.

explanation: Changing a real type or mode can replace the old configuration and initialize the new one with defaults. This pattern matches a report that assumes settings from the inactive mode must survive, although review accepts their replacement; examples include changing a form-field type, a webhook method or the selected issue-tracker mode. Verify that a genuine mode change occurred and what preservation is promised. Reselecting the same mode while secretly resetting values, or ignoring settings still saved for the active mode, is outside this rejection.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: In a repository's settings, choose the external issue tracker, fill in its URL, URL format and regex, and save. Switch to the built-in issue tracker and save. Choose the external issue tracker again and check its fields. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the external tracker's URL, format and regex are kept while the built-in tracker is in use, and reappear when switching back. It claimed this outcome: After switching to the built-in tracker and saving, then choosing the external tracker again, the external URL, URL format and regex fields were empty. Review concluded: Intended: the built-in and external issue trackers are separate repository units, and saving settings removes the unit that isn't in use, so the external tracker's settings are deleted by design rather than kept for later. The same applies to the external wiki.

explanation: Different search pages or modes can deliberately apply different matching rules. In the reviewed Gitea case, repository issue search offered Exact phrase matching, while the dashboard separately offered Words mode that can find separated query words. A report matches this mistake when it calls the phrase search broken solely because Words finds an item that Exact does not, without showing failure of the offered phrase operation. Compare the same query under the same supported mode; an incorrect mode label or a promised matching rule that fails is a separate defect.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: In repository Issues, search release proposal against an issue titled Review the release ownership proposal. Observe no result. Search ownership proposal and confirm the issue appears. On global Issues, search release proposal in default Exact mode and observe the same non-match. Switch global Issues to Words and observe the matching issue. The rejected report expected: The reporter expects release proposal to find an issue titled Review the release ownership proposal in repository issue search. It claimed this outcome: Repository search returns no result for release proposal but finds the adjacent phrase ownership proposal. Global Issues Exact also returns no result; choosing Words finds the issue. Review concluded: User rejected this search-only report. Scope is the reported comparison between repository phrase search and dashboard Words mode, not a blanket exclusion of search bugs. Repository issue search offers no search-mode selector and uses default Exact phrase matching; the supplied control establishes that the global default behaves the same. No failure of the offered phrase-search operation is established.
